en: Itivuttaka 14: Ekakanipāta, Second Chapter Thus it was said by the Blessed One, so I have heard: "Monks, there is one thing that, when developed and cultivated, leads to the abandoning of all things. What is that one thing? It is mindfulness of the body (*kāyagatāsati*). This, monks, is that one thing which, when developed and cultivated, leads to the abandoning of all things. Thus it was said by the Blessed One. Having said this, the Well-Gone One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then, soon after the Blessed One had departed, a certain monk approached the Venerable Ānanda and said to him: "Friend Ānanda, what is the name of this discourse spoken by the Blessed One? "It is called *Kāyagatāsati*, friend," he replied. "But, friend Ānanda, how is this discourse on *Kāyagatāsati* to be practiced? "In this way, friend, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body internally; he dwells contemplating the body in the body externally; he dwells contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the body; he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the body; he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the body. Mindful, he breathes in; mindful, he breathes out. Breathing in a long breath, he knows 'I breathe in a long breath'; breathing out a long breath, he knows 'I breathe out a long breath. Breathing in a short breath, he knows 'I breathe in a short breath'; breathing out a short breath, he knows 'I breathe out a short breath. Experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe in,' thus he trains himself; 'experiencing the whole body, I shall breathe out,' thus he trains himself. Calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe in,' thus he trains himself; 'calming the bodily formation, I shall breathe out,' thus he trains himself. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings internally; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings externally; he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in feelings; he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in feelings; he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in feelings. He dwells contemplating mind in mind internally; he dwells contemplating mind in mind externally; he dwells contemplating mind in mind both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in the mind; he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in the mind; he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in the mind. He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena internally; he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena externally; he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena both internally and externally. He dwells contemplating the nature of arising in phenomena; he dwells contemplating the nature of passing away in phenomena; he dwells contemplating the nature of both arising and passing away in phenomena. In this way, friend, this discourse on *Kāyagatāsati* is to be practiced. Thus spoke the Venerable Ānanda. Delighted, that monk rejoiced in the words of the Venerable Ānanda. The Discourse on the Hindrance of Ignorance.
This was said by the Blessed One, said by the Arahant; thus have I heard:
"Bhikkhus, I do not perceive even a single other hindrance by which beings, when hindered, wander and transmigrate for so long a time as this hindrance of ignorance, bhikkhus."
“Bhikkhus, shrouded by the hindrance of ignorance, beings wander and transmigrate for a long time.
Thus the Blessed One spoke. With reference to this, it is said:
“There is no other single thing by which mankind is so shrouded that they wander through saṃsāra day and night.”
Just as those who are enveloped by delusion,
so too are those who, having abandoned delusion,
have shattered the mass of darkness.
“They do not wander in saṃsāra again;
the cause for them no longer exists.
This meaning was also spoken by the Blessed One; thus have I heard.
